title: On Thinking Gray
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece contrasts black-and-white thinking, which sacrifices nuance for speed, with 'thinking gray,' a deliberate practice of weighing an issue's complexity before landing on a view. It emphasizes that thinking gray isn't indecision — it's a disciplined pause that seeks out strong opposing opinions before forming a judgment. The article notes this approach is best reserved for consequential decisions, since minor issues genuinely benefit from quick resolution. It closes with a warning that leaders who resist thinking gray do so at their own peril on important calls.
points: Black-and-white thinking sacrifices nuance and often produces poor decisions.
Thinking gray means deliberately weighing an issue's complexity before forming a judgment.
Thinking gray is not indecision — it's a disciplined pause, not a permanent state of ambivalence.
The approach requires actively seeking out strong opposing viewpoints before reaching a conclusion.
This deliberate approach is reserved for consequential decisions, not minor issues that benefit from speed.
quotes: Any time a leader oversimplifies a decision or issue by choosing to see things in extreme good’s and bad’s or right’s and wrong’s, they typically make poor choices and draw inadequate conclusions.
By giving up the middle ground, or shades of gray, leaders lose the flexibility to appreciate the complexity inherent in situations and people.
They care about understanding the factors at play that are obscure or lie underneath what is apparent on the face.
More specifically, thinking gray requires leaders to seek out strong and opposite opinions about an issue or experience.
Those who resist thinking gray do so at their own peril as decision-makers.
